Abstract We propose a fine-tuning method for flow-matching diffusion models aimed at realistic artificial light modeling without the need for a large training dataset. We address the task of controllable interior image editing, where the goal is to turn artificial light sources on or off while preserving the scene geometry, object placement, materials, and visual identity of the original image. To achieve this, we decompose the task into two independent formulations. We introduce the LoRA Direction Training Method, which extracts the pure direction of the LoRA adapter effect in the diffusion model flow field, and we also introduce specialized loss functions to ensure the realism of the inverse transformation. Additionally, the resulting increment map is used for more precise adjustment of the lighting color and temperature. 1 Introduction Modern image editing models demonstrate high quality across a wide range of transformations, including object insertion, style transfer, and global scene modification. However, artificial lighting control remains a challenging task. Altering the lighting can significantly transform an interior image. A model must not merely change the appearance of a lamp but also update the associated lighting effects in a physically and visually plausible manner. Turning on a lamp affects not only the local brightness near the light source but also the distribution of shadows, reflections, color tones, and the overall visual balance of the scene. Similarly, turning off the artificial light should result in a consistent change in both global and local illumination. At the same time, any unintended changes to the composition, object shapes, or materials are perceived as a disruption of the interior identity. Consequently, editing the lighting states is a more complex task than standard local editing based on text prompts. In this work, we approach the task of artificial light activation by treating the operation not as the addition of any new content, but as a change of the state of the already-existing scene — a concept formally akin to Style Transfer [ 21 ] . Activating a light can be viewed as a directed transformation of the visual state of the scene: the light source is already present in the image, but its activity level and the resulting illumination distribution change. This formulation allows the model to learn the controlled modification of the existing image element while preserving the identity of the interior rather than generating any arbitrary new content. However, turning off the artificial light is not a simple inverse transformation. When a light source is active, some information regarding shadows, local exposure, original material colors, and scene details may be distorted or lost. Therefore, in a computational context, turning off the light is less like an inverse style transfer and more akin to recovering an overexposed image, i.e., a task related to inpainting. This distinction motivates separate consideration of the tasks of turning the light on and off as related, but not entirely symmetrical, editing directions. For this reason, our solution employs two distinct adapters: one responsible for turning on the artificial light and the other for turning it off. This separation prevents the mixing up of fundamentally different tasks within a single training signal and allows for more precise control over the editing outcome. At the same time, adapter specialization enables operation in a data-constrained setting, thereby reducing the volume and complexity of training data preparation. Our work demonstrates that complex local light editing tasks can be addressed using relatively simple methods, provided the task is properly formulated and the approach is sufficiently decomposed. Rather than training a universal relighting model, we focus on a specific, practically relevant operation—changing the state of a particular artificial light source within an image—and show that even a small paired dataset can suffice to produce consistent and visually plausible results. 2 Related Work 2.1 Image Editing and Relighting Image relighting is traditionally regarded as changing the scene illumination after capture. Unlike standard local edits, this operation requires coordinated changes in brightness, shadows, highlights, reflections, and color tone, while preserving the geometry, materials, and identity of the original scene. Interior images present a particular challenge: unlike outdoor scenes with a dominant light source, indoor spaces typically contain multiple local and global light sources, complex inter-reflections, soft shadows, and heterogeneous materials. This issue is discussed in detail in ScribbleLight [ 7 ] , where the authors emphasize that indoor relighting is complicated by a mixture of natural and artificial light, occlusions, and complex light interactions in cluttered scenes. Early and physics-based approaches to relighting often rely on explicit modeling of geometry, materials, and lighting patterns. For instance, the SwitchLight [ 5 ] portrait relighting method employs a physically grounded architecture based on Cook-Torrance reflection models, decomposing the image into intrinsic components for subsequent rendering under target lighting. While this approach offers physically interpretable control, it is specialized for portraits and requires explicit surface property descriptions, making it difficult to generalize to complex interior scenes containing numerous objects and materials. Related research areas include harmonization and relighting techniques for image compositing. Relightful Harmonization [ 6 ] addresses the task of inserting a portrait subject into a new background by training a lighting-aware diffusion model; this model extracts lighting cues from the background image and uses them to harmonize the foreground lighting. The authors note that standard harmonization methods primarily adjust color, brightness, and contrast but often overlook lighting direction, intensity, and shadows, which can result in an unnatural-looking composite. Unlike such works, our task is not limited to harmonizing an object and a background; rather, it requires changing the state of light sources already present within a single scene. 2.2 Diffusion Models for Lighting Control With the advancement of generative models, an increasing number of studies treat relighting as a conditional image editing task. LightLab [ 8 ] proposes a diffusion-based method for the parametric control of light sources within a single image; the model is fine-tuned on a small set of real-world photo pairs—augmented by a significantly larger volume of synthetically rendered data—and leverages the linearity of light to synthesize controlled changes in light source intensity and color. This approach aligns with our problem formulation in that it addresses the modification of visible light sources and aims to provide explicit control over lighting parameters. However, LightLab relies on data augmentation via physically motivated synthetic rendering, whereas our work focuses on training a controllable LoRA adapter direction using a small paired dataset. ScribbleLight [ 7 ] also employs a diffusion model for interior relighting but introduces user control via scribble annotations. The method combines albedo-conditioned Stable Diffusion with ControlNet, deriving the control signal from sketches and surface normals; this enables localized lighting adjustments, such as toggling lights and adding highlights, shadows, and indirect illumination. Unlike ScribbleLight, our method does not require spatial user masks or sketches during training; at the inference process, control is achieved by selecting the target object with a bounding box on the source image following the implementation of the base model. ControlLight [ 9 ] treats lighting control as a task of controllable enhancement for low-light images. The method constructs a large-scale dataset Light100K : first, pseudo-paired normal-light targets are generated for real low-light images, and then intermediate states with varying lighting enhancement strengths are synthesized for each pair. For training, the authors employ FLUX.2-klein and fine-tune the diffusion model using LoRA; the enhancement strength parameter s s serves as the LoRA adapter scale, enabling continuous adjustment of the image brightening level. Additionally, a misalignment-aware weighted flow matching loss is introduced to mitigate the impact of regions with boundary mismatches in the pseudo-target pairs and to help preserve the scene structure. This approach resembles our work in that it also utilizes LoRA adaptation of a diffusion model for controllable lighting modification. However, ControlLight relies on a large pseudo-paired dataset and addresses the task of primarily global enhancement for low-light images by controlling the overall brightening strength. LuxRemix [ 10 ] proposes a method for interactive light editing in interior scenes by decomposing complex lighting into individual light source contributions—using a "One-Light-At-A-Time" (OLAT) format—and a background component. The method first trains a single-image lighting decomposition model, then propagates the resulting components across multiple scene views via multi-view lighting harmonization, and finally encodes the consistent lighting components into a relightable 3D Gaussian Splatting representation, allowing for interactive control over the intensity, color, and state of individual light sources. To train the single-image model, the authors use a large synthetic dataset comprising over 12,000 interior scenes featuring procedurally generated light sources and ground truth OLAT decompositions. The base model is a text-based image editing DiT fine-tuned using LoRA; the target source is specified via a spatial mask, while related tasks such as OLAT decomposition and turning off a selected source are distinguished by special text-based trigger words. This method is the closest to our solution given the problem formulation; however, it still relies on large datasets, complex annotation, and modification of the base model, whereas we utilize a small, carefully curated dataset and lightweight adapters. 2.3 Controllable Editing and LoRA Directions A distinct line of research focuses on identifying controllable directions within the parameter or latent space of diffusion models. Concept Sliders [ 11 ] propose training LoRA adapters as interpretable "sliders" for precise control over visual attributes. Such a slider corresponds to a low-rank parameter direction that amplifies a chosen concept while minimizing the impact on other attributes, allowing for continuous and modular control. Our work is conceptually similar, as it treats LoRA not merely as a fine-tuning mechanism but also as a controllable editing direction. However, unlike Concept Sliders, we extract the LoRA editing direction directly within the model’s flow/velocity field, linking two opposing scene states: lights on and lights off. LoRA of Change [ 12 ] is the work closest in spirit to ours. The authors view LoRA as a carrier of visual instructions derived from before-after pairs. Their method dynamically generates an instruction-specific LoRA from a single before-after pair and introduces LoRA Reverse Training to learn from paired data without requiring more complex quad sets. In contrast, however, we do not generate a LoRA for an arbitrary instruction using a hypernetwork; instead, we train a compact LoRA for a specific control operation and explicitly extract a signed direction in velocity/flow space via symmetric +s/-s passes. This enables the operation in a tiny-data regime and allows the sign of the adapter weight to serve as a control variable for toggling the scene state. 2.4 Flow Matching and FLUX.1 Kontext We use FLUX.1 Kontext [ 2 ] as our base model — a flow-matching [ 22 ] model designed for in-context image generation and editing within latent space. FLUX.1 Kontext integrates image generation and editing into a unified architecture that leverages both textual and visual context; it demonstrates strong performance in local and global editing, object identity preservation, and stability across multi-step edits. These characteristics make it a suitable foundation for interior editing tasks, which require altering the lighting while preserving the composition, geometry, and objects of the scene. Our work advances this line of research by treating the LoRA [ 1 ] adapter as a directional addition to the flow/velocity field of the base model. Unlike the standard application of LoRA as a static fine-tuning mechanism, we interpret the sign and scale as control parameters for editing of the adapter. A symmetric procedure involving +s and -s passes allows us to isolate the pure direction of the LoRA effect without relying on the zero-adapter state as a teacher. This is particularly crucial for lighting modification tasks, where the base model (without the adapter) does not necessarily define a correct neutral trajectory between the lights on and lights off states. Positioning Our Method Thus, the existing methods for image lighting control can be broadly categorized into three groups: physically motivated relighting approaches, diffusion-based methods utilizing external control signals, and controlled editing methods via LoRA directions. Physically motivated methods offer interpretability but often require specialized setups, additional scene representations, or complex data. Diffusion-based relighting methods provide a stronger photorealistic prior but typically rely on explicit masks, sketches, normal maps, large datasets, or parametric light source descriptions. LoRA-based methods enable the compact encoding of visual transformations; however, in most cases, they do not consider the problem formulation itself as a distinct factor determining the quality and robustness of the solution. Our method occupies an intermediate position between these directions. On the one hand, we use the photorealistic prior of a modern diffusion model and do not build an explicit physical model of the scene. On the other hand, we do not reduce the task to universal text editing, but clearly decompose it into two semantically related, but different in form transformations: turning on artificial light - changing the style, and turning it off - restoring the overexposed image. We focus on the correct formulation of the problem and its formalization to determine ways to implement the solution. We use Flux.1 Kontext as the base model, relying on its excellent ability to preserve details of the original scene during local image editing, and train two adapters with separate areas of application on its basis. For the task of turning on the light, we consider LoRA not just as a set of additional weights, but as a directional correction to the flow/velocity field of the base diffusion model. Unlike approaches where the adapter effect is assessed by comparing a model with and without LoRA, we perform two symmetric runs with positive and negative adapter scales. The LoRA edit direction is then extracted as the central difference between the corresponding flow/velocity fields. This avoids using the zero-adapter state as a teacher, which is especially important in cases where the base model does not specify the correct neutral direction for the target operation. The resulting direction is interpreted as a controllable addition to the flow field of the base model, responsible for transitioning the selected light source to the active state. To improve direction stability, we use an A/B training scheme that connects forward and reverse examples of lighting changes, as well as the loss function that combines supervised flow-matching loss and direction-tying loss. In this case, the negative adapter scale is used not as an independent solution to the task of turning off the light, but as a symmetric means of stabilizing and extracting the direction for the light-on operation. For the task of turning off the light, a separate LoRA adapter and a separate training set-up are used. It is based on the standard inpainting-like pipeline, but is complemented by a loss function specifically adapted to artificial light editing. This function enhances the contribution of areas associated with the light source and its effect on the scene, but does not completely nullify the background, so that the model continues to be signaled to preserve the geometry, materials and composition of the frame. Additionally, low-frequency matching of the predicted and target flow fields is used, which penalizes errors in global exposure, color temperature and shadow distribution. Thanks to this, the adapter learns not just to darken the lamp area, but to consistently restore the visual state of the scene after removing the contribution of the artificial source. The key difference of our method lies not in making the architecture more complex, but in combining three simple solutions: using a strong base image-editing model, training compact LoRA adapters on a small paired dataset, and formulating the light-on and light-off tasks separately. This approach enables local editing of artificial lighting without large composite datasets, complex physical scene reconstruction, dense masks, sketch annotations, or multi-view capture, while preserving the controllability of the result and the identity of the original interior. In view of the above, it is important to emphasize that we use the control bounding box only at the inference stage, and it is not part of the LoRA adapter training signal. During training, the target light source is specified exclusively by a text instruction, and the source images are not supplemented with masks, boxes, or other spatial annotations. At the inference stage, the selected luminaire is spatially localized using the existing capabilities of the base FLUX.1 Kontext model. Thus, the adapter learns the direction of the lighting-state change itself, while the mechanism for selecting a specific object remains with the base image-editing model. 3 Dataset In this work, we were limited in our ability to prepare and utilize a large-scale training dataset. Consequently, we sought to compensate for the limited sample size by prioritizing the quality and controllability of the constituent examples. This resulted in the creation of a paired dataset comprising approximately 320 image pairs. The majority (around 90 % 90\% ) of the dataset consisted of specially prepared synthetic examples, while the remaining 10 % 10\% comprised real-world photographs. This approach allowed us to augment the controlled synthetic samples with examples featuring natural light and shadow distributions. Each image pair depicts the same scene under two different artificial lighting conditions and is used to construct corresponding forward and reverse training examples. This format enables control over the state of a selected light source while preserving the geometry, materials, and overall composition of the scene. It is important to note that the training dataset consisted exclusively of interior scenes. Thus, at the current stage of the method development, its intended application is limited to editing artificial light sources located indoors. Nevertheless, a number of exterior scenes were deliberately included in the final test set to better evaluate the generalization limits of the method. See examples of the method performance in Appendices A and B. 3.1 Synthetic Data The synthetic subset was generated using specially selected, high-resolution, detailed interior scenes processed to closely approximate the visual characteristics of real-world photographs. To increase the diversity of lighting sources, the synthetic portion of the dataset was divided into several categories corresponding to the most common types of interior light fixtures found in residential and public spaces: • Table lamps ( table ); • Ceiling lights ( ceiling ); • Floor lamps ( floor ); • Linear interior lights ( linear ); • Pendant lights ( pendant ); • Wall lights ( wall ). However, the dataset does not include light sources that are specialized or atypical for the interior layouts under consideration, such as decorative multi-lamp chandeliers, candle-shaped bulbs, or industrial and medical fluorescent fixtures. Each category comprises scenes featuring the respective light sources under varying environmental conditions and focal lengths, and with varying degrees of contribution to the overall illumination of the room. Consequently, the dataset encompasses both local light sources which primarily affect nearby surfaces and more prominent sources that significantly alter the global lighting balance of the scene. This categorization aims to increase the diversity of geometry and artificial light propagation patterns within the unified training dataset. 3.2 Real world data Real-world image pairs of lamps and light fixtures captured in natural settings account for approximately 10 % 10\% of the training dataset. Unlike the synthetic component, generating this data requires capturing the same scene under varying artificial lighting conditions. Moreover, when working with very small datasets, alignment errors such as those caused by a camera shake during capture can have catastrophic consequences for the final adapter. This makes collecting real-world pairs significantly more labor-intensive than collecting and annotating individual images. Consequently, this portion of the dataset is limited in both the total number of images and the diversity of light source types represented. Despite their smaller volume and less controlled capture conditions, real-world images play a crucial role in training. Since light is a complex physical phenomenon its modeling in synthetic scenes inevitably entails limitations regarding the accurate reproduction of light transport. Even with highly realistic rendering, the lighting distribution in synthetic data may remain more regular and predictable than in real-world photographs. In contrast, real-world images directly reflect the actual behavior of light within a scene, including the interaction of multiple sources, reflections from various materials, shadow non-uniformity, local exposure variations, and other effects that are difficult to fully replicate through synthetic generation. Thus, the synthetic and real-world components of the dataset serve complementary functions. Synthetic data provides precise control over paired scene states and increases the diversity of training examples, while real-world photographs help bridge the gap between synthetic and real-world lighting distributions. 4 Light-On 4.1 Task Formulation Let’s consider the task of controllable image editing that involves turning on artificial light sources in a scene. Let a set of paired examples be given. 𝒟 = { ( x i 0 , x i 1 , p i + , p i − ) } i = 1 N , \mathcal{D}=\{(x_{i}^{0},x_{i}^{1},p_{i}^{+},p_{i}^{-})\}_{i=1}^{N}, where x i 0 x_{i}^{0} denotes the initial scene image without the target lighting effect or with the light source turned off, and x i 1 x_{i}^{1} denotes an image of the same scene after the artificial lighting is turned on. The text conditions p i + p_{i}^{+} and p i − p_{i}^{-} describe, respectively, the forward operation of turning on the light and the reverse operation of restoring the initial state. We consider a conditional diffusion model for image editing in which the context image c c defines the preserved scene structure, while the target image x x defines the editing result. Pairs used for forward task A A c A = x 0 , x A = x 1 , p A = p + , c_{A}=x^{0},\qquad x_{A}=x^{1},\qquad p_{A}=p^{+}, and for inverse task B B : c B = x 1 , x B = x 0 , p B = p − . c_{B}=x^{1},\qquad x_{B}=x^{0},\qquad p_{B}=p^{-}. A distinctive feature of the task at hand is that turning on artificial light is not merely a matter of locally altering the color or brightness of a specific object. It necessitates a coordinated shift in the illumination distribution of the scene involving the appearance of a light spot, the over-illumination of nearby surfaces, shadows, reflections, color shifts, and contrast changes. In practice, a baseline model often lacks a robust representation of this operation: it might add a visible light source without physically consistent effects on the surroundings, modify textures rather than lighting, or interpret the request to turn on the light as a standard object-level edit. The objective is to train a LoRA adapter with parameter ϕ \phi that defines a controllable editing direction. A positive adapter multiplier corresponds to the turn on light operation, whereas a negative multiplier is employed solely during training to evaluate and stabilize the LoRA-induced direction. We do not treat the negative scaling of this adapter as the primary mechanism for turning the light off. Consequently, beyond the standard supervised editing loss, a key element of the formulation is the requirement for directional consistency in the LoRA-induced change. We formulate this requirement as directional consistency regularization : the direction of change that the LoRA introduces into the model velocity field for the forward operation must be consistent with the direction for the reverse operation. For the task of turning lights on and off, this consistency is antisymmetric in nature. 4.2 Method Let ℰ \mathcal{E} denote the VAE encoder that maps an image x x to a latent representation. z = ℰ ⁡ ( x ) . z=\mathcal{E}(x). During the training step, a timestep t t and noise ϵ \epsilon are selected. The scheduler determines the noisy latent. z t = q t ​ ( z , ϵ ) , z_{t}=q_{t}(z,\epsilon), where the specific form of q t q_{t} is determined by the flow-matching or diffusion parameterization employed. The Flux Kontext [ 2 ] model takes a noisy latent, a timestep, a text condition, and a context image as input. Let us denote its prediction as v θ , ϕ ​ ( z t , t , p , c , a ) , v_{\theta,\phi}(z_{t},t,p,c;a), where θ \theta denotes the frozen parameters of the base model, ϕ \phi denotes the trainable LoRA parameters, and a a denotes the scalar multiplier of the adapter. The key idea of the method is to explicitly isolate the direction that LoRA adds to the velocity field predicted by the model. To do this, we use the symmetric difference between two predictions computed on the same input but with opposite adapter multipliers. For a fixed s > 0 s>0 , we define the LoRA-induced direction: Δ ϕ ​ ( z t , t , p , c ) = v θ , ϕ ​ ( z t , t , p , c , + s ) − v θ , ϕ ​ ( z t , t , p , c , − s ) 2 ​ s . \Delta_{\phi}(z_{t},t,p,c)=\frac{v_{\theta,\phi}(z_{t},t,p,c;+s)-v_{\theta,\phi}(z_{t},t,p,c;-s)}{2s}. Both predictions in the numerator are computed using the same z t z_{t} , t t , ϵ \epsilon , p p , and c c ; only the sign of the adapter multiplier differs. Such a central difference suppresses the common component of the base model and estimates the local LoRA-induced direction in the model prediction space. For forward task A A and inverse task B B , we obtain: Δ A = v A ​ ( + s ) − v A ​ ( − s ) 2 ​ s , Δ B = v B ​ ( + s ) − v B ​ ( − s ) 2 ​ s . \Delta_{A}=\frac{v_{A}(+s)-v_{A}(-s)}{2s},\qquad\Delta_{B}=\frac{v_{B}(+s)-v_{B}(-s)}{2s}. Since the forward and backward passes are computed for a single training pair with consistent values of t t and ϵ \epsilon , Δ A \Delta_{A} and Δ B \Delta_{B} can be viewed as coupled estimates of the LoRA-induced response for two opposing states of the same scene. ℒ dir = ‖ Δ A + Δ B ‖ 2 2 . \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{dir}}=\left\|\Delta_{A}+\Delta_{B}\right\|_{2}^{2}. The concept of using forward and inverse transformations as mutually consistent training signals traces back to earlier works on cycle consistency, specifically CycleGAN [ 19 ] . In our work, this principle is not applied directly but is instead reinterpreted for modern flow-matching image-editing models and LoRA parameterization. Unlike classical cycle consistency, we do not construct an explicit closed loop where the output of the forward transformation serves as the input for the inverse transformation to reconstruct the original image. Instead, the forward and inverse tasks are trained on the corresponding ground-truth pairs, and their mutual consistency is enforced at the level of LoRA-induced directions within the flow/velocity field of the model. Thus, rather than requiring F ⁡ ( G ⁡ ( x ) ) ≈ x F(G(x))\approx x , we employ an antisymmetric constraint— Δ A ≈ − Δ B \Delta_{A}\approx-\Delta_{B} , which is more natural for our formulation; this constraint links the model’s responses for opposite directions of the scene state change. We utilize this coupling as a regularizer. Its role is to encourage opposing response trends in the model prediction space for the forward and reverse operations, thereby establishing a more robust editing direction associated with changes in the light source state. Without such a constraint, the supervised loss could be satisfied through localized color or texture changes without forming a coherent representation of the target operation. In addition to directional consistency regularization, we employ the standard supervised flow-matching loss [ 22 ] . For the forward task: ℒ A = ℓ ⁡ ( v A ​ ( + s ) , u A ) , \mathcal{L}_{A}=\ell\left(v_{A}(+s),u_{A}\right), where u A u_{A} is the target velocity/flow value determined by the scheduler. For reverse pairs, an additional auxiliary supervised term may be used: ℒ B = ℓ ⁡ ( v B ​ ( − s ) , u B ) . \mathcal{L}_{B}=\ell\left(v_{B}(-s),u_{B}\right). The final loss function has the form ℒ = w A ​ ℒ A + w B ​ ℒ B + w dir ​ ℒ dir , \mathcal{L}=w_{A}\mathcal{L}_{A}+w_{B}\mathcal{L}_{B}+w_{\mathrm{dir}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{dir}}, where w A w_{A} , w B w_{B} , and w dir w_{\mathrm{dir}} specify the weights for the forward supervised loss, the backward supervised loss, and the directional consistency regularization, respectively. Crucially, the method does not use the base model prediction—with LoRA disabled—as a teacher. In tasks involving turning on artificial light, such a prediction often serves as an unreliable reference point, as the base model may not grasp the act of turning on the light as a physically consistent redistribution of scene illumination. Instead, we compare two symmetric states of the same LoRA, + s +s and − s -s ; this allows us to learn a directed and controllable change in the velocity field rather than an absolute correction relative to relatively weak behavior of the base model. It is important to emphasize that, in this formulation, inverse pairs serve as an auxiliary regularization signal that stabilizes the learned editing direction. At the inference stage, turning off the light is not achieved by applying a negative scale to the Light-On adapter; instead, a separate Light-Off adapter with its own formulation and loss function is trained for that operation. 5 Light-Off 5.1 Task Formulation We consider the task of conditional image editing, which involves turning off an artificial light source while preserving the scene geometry, object materials, and frame composition. Let x i on x_{i}^{\mathrm{on}} denote the original image of the scene with the light source on, and x i off x_{i}^{\mathrm{off}} denote the target image of the same scene after the light source is turned off. The training set is defined by a collection of pairs 𝒟 = { ( x i on , x i off , p i , m i ) } i = 1 N , \mathcal{D}=\left\{\left(x_{i}^{\mathrm{on}},x_{i}^{\mathrm{off}},p_{i},m_{i}\right)\right\}_{i=1}^{N}, where p i p_{i} is a text editing instruction, and m i m_{i} is an optional spatial loss weight map. The goal is to learn the parameters of adapter ϕ \phi which, when added to a fixed pre-trained conditional editing model F θ 0 F_{\theta_{0}} , implements the transformation T ϕ : x on ↦ x off . T_{\phi}:x^{\mathrm{on}}\mapsto x^{\mathrm{off}}. In this process, the parameters of the base model θ 0 \theta_{0} remain unchanged, and only the low-rank LoRA increment is trained. θ ⁡ ( ϕ ) = θ 0 + Δ ​ θ ϕ . \theta(\phi)=\theta_{0}+\Delta\theta_{\phi}. Unlike localized tasks such as object removal or replacement, turning off a light source requires altering the global lighting, specifically brightness, color temperature, shadows, reflected light, and the glow of the source itself. Consequently, the task cannot be reduced to simply darkening the area around the lamp. Furthermore, the scene identity, including object positions and shapes, materials, textures, and overall composition, must be preserved. It is also important to note that the inverse transformation ( x off ↦ x on x^{\mathrm{off}}\mapsto x^{\mathrm{on}} ) is not strictly reversible in the general case. A single image with the light source turned off could correspond to various lighting configurations, intensities, and reflection conditions. Therefore, the task is primarily framed as a unidirectional editing task ( x on → x off x^{\mathrm{on}}\rightarrow x^{\mathrm{off}} ) rather than the learning of a symmetric pair of mutually inverse transformations. 5.2 Method We use a pre-trained model for conditional image editing in latent space. Let E E denote the VAE encoder that maps an image to a latent representation. This protocol allows for the separate assessment of visual quality of the result, the accuracy of the requested lighting modification, and the plausibility of the generated image.
